- Step 3 (normalized bump) becomes dbr_normalized_bump.
- Step 4 (antiderivative) becomes dbr_antiderivative: a zero-mean continuous function compactly supported in (a, b) has a compactly supported C¹ antiderivative.

(2) If a < b, dbr_normalized_bump gives η: C^∞, compact support, tsupport ⊆ (a, b) and ∫η = 1. Put c := ∫ηκ.
(3) Fix a C^∞ χ with compact support and tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b). Let I := ∫χ and χ₀ := χ − I·η.
  - χ₀ is continuous and has compact support (HasCompactSupport.sub and mul_left).
  - tsupport χ₀ ⊆ tsupport χ ∪ tsupport η ⊆ (a, b) (tsupport_sub, tsupport_mul_subset_right).
  - ∫χ₀ = I − I·1 = 0, because χ and η are continuous with compact support and hence integrable.
  - dbr_antiderivative gives Φ: C¹, compact support, tsupport Φ ⊆ (a, b), deriv Φ = χ₀.
  - The hypothesis applied to Φ gives 0 = ∫χ₀κ = ∫χκ − I·c. This uses integrability of χκ and ηκ from dbr_integrable.
  - Hence ∫χ(κ − c) = ∫χκ − c·I = 0.
(4) dbr_fundamental_lemma applied to g := κ − c, which is continuous on (a, b), gives κ = c on (a, b).

subproblems.title: Integrability of a compactly supported continuous function times a function continuous on (a, b)
subproblems.statement: Let a, b be reals and κ, χ : ℝ → ℝ. Suppose κ is continuous on the open interval (a, b), χ is continuous on ℝ, χ has compact support, and tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b). Then the function x ↦ χ(x)·κ(x) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (a b : ℝ) (κ χ : ℝ → ℝ), ContinuousOn κ (Ioo a b) → Continuous χ → HasCompactSupport χ → tsupport χ ⊆ Ioo a b → Integrable (fun x => χ x * κ x)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 2 (Integrability) of the parent proof of the du Bois-Reymond lemma, stated here for an arbitrary continuous χ. Lebesgue measure on ℝ is `volume`.
1. Let K := tsupport χ, the closure of the support of χ. Because χ has compact support, K is compact, and K ⊆ (a, b) by hypothesis. No assumption a < b is needed: if K = ∅ the argument below applies verbatim.
2. κ is continuous on (a, b), hence on its subset K (ContinuousOn.mono with K ⊆ (a, b)). χ is continuous on ℝ, hence on K. So the product x ↦ χ(x)κ(x) is continuous on K (ContinuousOn.mul).
3. Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets and ℝ is Hausdorff. So a function continuous on the compact set K is integrable on K (ContinuousOn.integrableOn_compact), i.e. IntegrableOn (fun x => χ x * κ x) K.
4. If x ∉ K = tsupport χ, then χ(x) = 0 (image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport), so χ(x)κ(x) = 0·κ(x) = 0.
5. A function that is integrable on K and vanishes at every point outside K is integrable on ℝ (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero, using steps 3 and 4). Hence x ↦ χ(x)κ(x) is integrable on ℝ. ∎
proof_key_steps: K := tsupport χ is compact and K ⊆ (a, b).
χ·κ is continuous on K, hence integrable on the compact set K.
χ·κ vanishes outside K, hence is integrable on ℝ.

subproblems.title: Normalized smooth bump in an open interval
subproblems.statement: For all reals a < b there is a C^∞ function η : ℝ → ℝ with compact support, tsupport η ⊆ (a, b), and ∫_ℝ η(x) dx = 1.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (a b : ℝ), a < b → ∃ η : ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) η ∧ HasCompactSupport η ∧ tsupport η ⊆ Ioo a b ∧ ∫ x, η x = 1
proof_key_steps: Take the ContDiffBump β centred at (a+b)/2 with radii (b−a)/8 and (b−a)/4.
∫β > 0 because β ≥ 0 is integrable and its support is an interval of positive length.
η := (∫β)⁻¹·β is C^∞, compactly supported in (a, b), with ∫η = 1.

subproblems.title: Compactly supported C¹ antiderivative of a zero-mean continuous function
subproblems.statement: Let a, b be reals and g : ℝ → ℝ continuous with compact support, tsupport g ⊆ (a, b) and ∫_ℝ g(x) dx = 0. Then there is Φ : ℝ → ℝ of class C¹ with compact support, tsupport Φ ⊆ (a, b), and deriv Φ = g (equality of functions).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (a b : ℝ) (g : ℝ → ℝ), Continuous g → HasCompactSupport g → tsupport g ⊆ Ioo a b → ∫ x, g x = 0 → ∃ Φ : ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 Φ ∧ HasCompactSupport Φ ∧ tsupport Φ ⊆ Ioo a b ∧ deriv Φ = g
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 (Antiderivatives) of the parent proof of the du Bois-Reymond lemma, applied to an arbitrary g in place of χ₀ = χ − (∫χ)η. Lebesgue measure on ℝ is `volume`, and ∫_{u}^{v} denotes the oriented interval integral.
1. Let K := tsupport g. K is compact (g has compact support) and K ⊆ (a, b).
   If K = ∅, every x lies outside tsupport g, so g(x) = 0 for all x (image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport), i.e. g = 0. Then Φ := 0 works: it is C¹ (constant), has compact support, tsupport 0 = ∅ ⊆ (a, b), and deriv 0 = 0 = g. This case also covers b ≤ a, since then (a, b) = ∅. Assume from now on K ≠ ∅.
2. Choose a′ and b′.
   - A nonempty compact subset of ℝ contains its infimum and supremum (IsCompact.sInf_mem, IsCompact.sSup_mem). So k₁ := inf K ∈ K and k₂ := sup K ∈ K, hence a < k₁ and k₂ < b.
   - Put a′ := (a + k₁)/2 and b′ := (k₂ + b)/2. Then a < a′ < k₁ ≤ k₂ < b′ < b.
   - K is bounded, so every y ∈ K satisfies k₁ ≤ y ≤ k₂ (csInf_le, le_csSup); hence K ⊆ (a′, b′).
   - Consequently support g ⊆ K ⊆ (a′, b′), i.e. g(y) = 0 whenever y ≤ a′ or y ≥ b′.
3. Define Φ(x) := ∫_{a′}^{x} g(y) dy. Since g is continuous, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives HasStrictDerivAt Φ (g x) x for every x (Continuous.integral_hasStrictDerivAt with lower limit a′). So Φ is differentiable at every x, and deriv Φ x = g x (Continuous.deriv_integral). Thus Φ is differentiable on ℝ and deriv Φ = g, which is continuous; by contDiff_one_iff_deriv, Φ is C¹.
4. Φ vanishes outside [a′, b′].
   (i) If x < a′: the oriented integral ∫_{a′}^{x} g involves only points of the half-open interval uIoc a′ x = (x, a′]. Each such y satisfies y ≤ a′, so g(y) = 0 by step 2. Hence Φ(x) = 0 (intervalIntegral.integral_zero_ae).
   (ii) If x > b′: support g ⊆ (a′, b′) ⊆ (a′, x]. So ∫_{a′}^{x} g = ∫_ℝ g (intervalIntegral.integral_eq_integral_of_support_subset), which is 0 by hypothesis. Hence Φ(x) = 0.
5. By step 4, support Φ ⊆ [a′, b′].
   - [a′, b′] is compact, so Φ has compact support (HasCompactSupport.intro).
   - [a′, b′] is closed, so tsupport Φ = closure(support Φ) ⊆ [a′, b′] (closure_minimal).
   - [a′, b′] ⊆ (a, b) because a < a′ and b′ < b.
   Together with step 3 (Φ is C¹ and deriv Φ = g), Φ has all the required properties. ∎
proof_key_steps: If tsupport g = ∅ then g = 0 and Φ = 0 works.
Otherwise choose a < a′ < inf K ≤ sup K < b′ < b, so g = 0 outside (a′, b′).
Φ(x) := ∫_{a′}^{x} g is C¹ with deriv Φ = g by the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Φ = 0 for x < a′ (g = 0 there) and for x > b′ (∫_ℝ g = 0), so Φ has compact support and tsupport Φ ⊆ [a′, b′] ⊆ (a, b).

subproblems.title: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations on an open interval (continuous version)
subproblems.statement: Let a, b be reals and g : ℝ → ℝ continuous on (a, b). Suppose ∫_ℝ χ(x)·g(x) dx = 0 for every C^∞ function χ : ℝ → ℝ with compact support and tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b). Then g(x) = 0 for every x ∈ (a, b).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (a b : ℝ) (g : ℝ → ℝ), ContinuousOn g (Ioo a b) → (∀ χ : ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) χ → HasCompactSupport χ → tsupport χ ⊆ Ioo a b → ∫ x, χ x * g x = 0) → ∀ x ∈ Ioo a b, g x = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 6 (Fundamental lemma) of the parent proof of the du Bois-Reymond lemma, with κ − c replaced by an arbitrary g. This is the basic version of the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations; Wikipedia, 'Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations', proves it with a bump on a subinterval where the function keeps one sign. Lebesgue measure on ℝ is `volume`. The proof uses the sibling lemma dbr_integrable.
1. Fix x₀ ∈ (a, b). We first prove the Claim: if h : ℝ → ℝ is continuous on (a, b) and ∫ χ(y)h(y) dy = 0 for every C^∞ χ with compact support and tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b), then h(x₀) > 0 is impossible.
2. Proof of the Claim. Suppose d := h(x₀) > 0.
   - (a, b) is open and contains x₀, so continuity of h on (a, b) gives continuity of h at x₀ (ContinuousOn.continuousAt with isOpen_Ioo.mem_nhds).
   - Both (a, b) and {y : h(y) > d/2} are neighbourhoods of x₀; the latter because d/2 < h(x₀) and h is continuous at x₀.
   - So there is ρ > 0 such that every y with |y − x₀| < ρ satisfies y ∈ (a, b) and h(y) > d/2 (Metric.eventually_nhds_iff_ball).
   - Put r := ρ/2. Then every y with |y − x₀| ≤ r satisfies y ∈ (a, b) and h(y) > d/2.
3. Let χ be the ContDiffBump centred at x₀ with inner radius r/2 and outer radius r (valid since 0 < r/2 < r; ℝ has HasContDiffBump ℝ). Then:
   - χ is C^∞, continuous, and has compact support;
   - 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, and χ(y) = 1 for |y − x₀| ≤ r/2 (one_of_mem_closedBall);
   - support χ = (x₀ − r, x₀ + r) and tsupport χ = [x₀ − r, x₀ + r];
   - tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b) by step 2.
   The hypothesis on h therefore gives ∫ χ(y)h(y) dy = 0.
4. χh ≥ 0 everywhere. If |y − x₀| ≤ r, then χ(y) ≥ 0 and h(y) > d/2 > 0, so χ(y)h(y) ≥ 0. Otherwise y ∉ (x₀ − r, x₀ + r) = support χ, so χ(y) = 0 and χ(y)h(y) = 0.
5. χh is integrable on ℝ by the sibling lemma dbr_integrable, applied with κ := h (continuous on (a, b)) and the continuous, compactly supported χ with tsupport χ ⊆ (a, b).
6. For |y − x₀| < r/2 we have χ(y) = 1 and h(y) > d/2 > 0, so χ(y)h(y) > d/2 > 0. Hence the support of χh contains the open interval (x₀ − r/2, x₀ + r/2), whose Lebesgue measure is r > 0 (Real.volume_ball and measure_mono). By integral_pos_iff_support_of_nonneg (χh ≥ 0 by step 4, integrable by step 5, support of positive measure), ∫χh > 0; quantitatively ∫χh ≥ (d/2)·r. This contradicts step 3 and proves the Claim.
7. Apply the Claim with h := g: g(x₀) > 0 is impossible.
   Apply it with h := −g. −g is continuous on (a, b), and for every admissible χ, ∫χ(−g) = −∫χg = 0 (mul_neg, integral_neg). So −g(x₀) > 0 is impossible, i.e. g(x₀) < 0 is impossible.
   By trichotomy g(x₀) = 0. Since x₀ ∈ (a, b) was arbitrary, g = 0 on (a, b). If b ≤ a the statement is vacuous. ∎
Remark (alternative Lean route, also complete). This proof can replace steps 1–7.
   - g is continuous on the measurable set (a, b), hence locally integrable on the open set (a, b) (ContinuousOn.locallyIntegrableOn with measurableSet_Ioo).
   - Mathlib's IsOpen.ae_eq_zero_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq_zero (Mathlib/Analysis/Distribution/AEEqOfIntegralContDiff.lean, reachable from the frozen imports) applies with μ := volume and U := (a, b). Its hypothesis ∫ χ • g = 0 is exactly the given one, since χ • g = χ·g (smul_eq_mul).
   - It yields ∀ᵐ x, x ∈ (a, b) → g x = 0, i.e. g = 0 almost everywhere for volume restricted to (a, b) (ae_restrict_iff' with measurableSet_Ioo).
   - g and the constant 0 are continuous on the open set (a, b), and Lebesgue measure is positive on nonempty open sets. So Measure.eqOn_open_of_ae_eq gives g x = 0 for every x ∈ (a, b).
proof_key_steps: It suffices to show that h(x₀) > 0 is impossible for any h satisfying the hypotheses; apply this to g and −g.
By continuity at x₀, find r > 0 with [x₀ − r, x₀ + r] ⊆ (a, b) and h > h(x₀)/2 there.
Take the ContDiffBump χ at x₀ with radii r/2 and r. Then χh ≥ 0, χh is integrable (dbr_integrable), and χh > h(x₀)/2 on (x₀ − r/2, x₀ + r/2).
Hence ∫χh > 0, contradicting the hypothesis ∫χh = 0; so g(x₀) = 0.
